name: russian tea cakes
instructions:
Classic russian tea cakes — also known as mexican wedding cookies or snowball cookies. Small buttery walnut cookies rolled twice in powdered sugar for the pristine white 'snowball' coating. Very few ingredients, very simple technique; the whole thing lives on butter + nuts + the double-roll finish.

MAKES ~3 dozen small cookies. 350°F oven.

=== INGREDIENTS ===

- 1 cup (2 sticks / 226g) unsalted butter, SOFTENED to room temp
- 1/2 cup powdered sugar, plus MORE AS NEEDED for the coating (~1 cup extra for rolling)
- 1 tsp vanilla extract
- 2 1/4 cups all-purpose flour
- 1/4 tsp table salt
- 3/4 cup crushed walnuts (finely chopped, not powder — see notes)

=== PROCEDURE (DEFAULT — COLD BUTTER, PIE-CRUST METHOD) ===

1. PREHEAT oven to 350°F.

2. WHISK DRY: in a large bowl, whisk together the flour, 1/2 cup powdered sugar, and salt.

3. CUT IN COLD BUTTER + VANILLA (PIE-CRUST STYLE): cut the cold butter into small cubes. Add to the dry ingredients along with the vanilla. Rub/mix by hand until the mixture resembles rustic sand or coarse crumbs (same technique as making pie crust). No creaming, no waiting for room-temp butter — this is the going-forward default method (see notes on why).

4. ADD WALNUTS: mix in the crushed walnuts by hand until distributed.

5. SHAPE INTO BALLS: press and roll the dough into ~1-inch balls. The dough should be firm enough from the cold butter that no chilling is needed. Place on an ungreased baking sheet — no need to leave much space; these don't spread much.

6. BAKE ~12-15 min at 350°F until SET but not browned. The bottoms should be lightly golden; the tops stay pale. Don't over-bake — they should look almost undercooked.

7. FIRST ROLL (WHILE WARM): let cookies cool ~5 min on the pan (still warm to the touch, but not scorching). Roll each cookie in powdered sugar to coat. The warmth helps the sugar stick — this is the FIRST coat.

8. COOL COMPLETELY on a rack.

9. SECOND ROLL (WHEN COOL): roll each cookie in powdered sugar AGAIN once fully cool. The second coat is what gives the pristine snowball appearance — the first coat melted slightly into the warm cookie; the second coat sits on top and stays white.

=== ALTERNATIVE PROCEDURE — CREAMED SOFTENED BUTTER (STANDARD METHOD) ===

Most recipes online use this method. Works fine but requires waiting for butter to soften. Kept here for reference.

1. PREHEAT oven to 350°F.
2. CREAM BUTTER + SUGAR + VANILLA: beat the SOFTENED butter with the 1/2 cup powdered sugar and vanilla until light and fluffy (~2-3 min). Butter must be at room temp.
3. STIR IN FLOUR + SALT + WALNUTS: add and mix until dough comes together. Should be soft but not sticky.
4. CHILL IF NEEDED: if the dough is too soft to shape, refrigerate 20-30 min.
5. Continue with steps 5-9 above (shape, bake, double roll).

Store in an airtight container. Keep well several days at room temp.
notes:
Classic russian tea cakes / mexican wedding cookies / snowball cookies. Same cookie, different regional names.

=== COLD BUTTER + PIE-CRUST METHOD IS THE DEFAULT (COOK-CONFIRMED) ===

Most recipes online insist on softened / room-temperature butter for the creaming step. I tried the cold-butter pie-crust method instead — cubed cold butter cut into a flour + powdered sugar + salt mix by hand, with vanilla added at the rubbing stage — and it turned out great. This is the going-forward default for me.

WHY IT WORKS: russian tea cakes are structurally closer to shortbread than to typical cookies (no eggs, low sugar, high butter). Shortbread and pie-crust doughs both build the same way — fat cut into dry ingredients, no creaming, no leavening — so it makes sense that the same technique lands here. Cutting cold butter into the dry gets the fat evenly distributed through the flour without needing a creaming step to introduce air (there's no leavener that would benefit from creamed-in air anyway).

ADVANTAGES over the softened-butter creaming method:
- No waiting for butter to reach room temp — start immediately with butter straight from the fridge.
- No creaming step — mix by hand or with a fork.
- Dough comes out firm enough to shape without chilling.
- Same finished cookie (indistinguishable in the finished bake).

Same technique family as [[greek-yogurt-lemon-pound-cake]]'s cold-cubed-butter-into-dry step. The cold-butter-pie-crust approach is worth knowing as a general tool for buttery baked goods that don't need creamed-in air.

SOFTENED-BUTTER CREAMING METHOD IS STILL VALID: kept in the ALTERNATIVE PROCEDURE section above. Works fine; just slower and requires planning ahead.

=== WALNUTS FINELY CHOPPED — NOT POWDERED, NOT WHOLE ===

Crush the walnuts to a fine chop — small pieces distributed through every cookie, but not so fine that they become walnut flour. Whole or halved walnuts don't work (too big; can't shape into 1-inch balls). Powdered / food-processor-blitzed walnuts lose the textural contribution — they become flour rather than nut inclusion.

PECANS work as a substitute for walnuts — traditional in the mexican wedding cookie version. Almonds also work but read slightly different (sweeter, less earthy). Walnuts are the classic russian pick.

=== THE DOUBLE ROLL IS LOAD-BEARING FOR THE SNOWBALL LOOK ===

Roll in powdered sugar TWICE:
1. FIRST ROLL while cookies are still WARM (5 min after out of the oven). The residual heat causes the sugar to partially melt into the surface — this is what makes the sugar STICK.
2. SECOND ROLL when cookies are FULLY COOL. The second coat sits on top and stays pristine white — this is what makes them look like snowballs.

Skip the first roll and the second coat won't stick as well. Skip the second roll and the cookies look grayish/uneven (from the melted-in first coat). Both rolls together = the pristine snowball appearance.

=== DON'T OVER-BAKE — SET, NOT BROWN ===

The cookies should look almost undercooked when they come out. Bottoms lightly golden; tops still pale. Over-baking pushes them into dry crumbly territory (the low sugar content doesn't caramelize much, so browning happens all at once). Pull them when they look barely done and let carryover finish them.

=== NO EGGS ===

Worth naming: this recipe has NO EGGS. All the binding comes from butter + flour + the mechanical shape. Different structural logic from most cookies — closer to shortbread.

=== CHILL THE DOUGH IF SOFT ===

If the dough is too soft to shape into balls (butter got too warm, or your kitchen is warm), refrigerate 20-30 min and try again. The dough should be firm enough to roll into balls that hold their shape.

=== SIBLING RECIPES / RELATED ===

- No sibling cookie recipes in this cookbook yet. Related in category to shortbread traditions (butter + flour, no eggs) rather than typical drop cookies (which usually have eggs).
